      CASE NO: 24VECV01479 

 

[TENTATIVE] RULING RE: CROSS-COMPLAINANT LOS ANGELES UNIFIED SCHOOL DISTRICT’S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT OR, ALTERNATIVELY, FOR SUMMARY ADJUDICATION OF ISSUES IN THE CROSS-COMPLAINT 

 

Dept. U 

8:30 a.m. 

August 5, 2026 

 

A. BACKGROUND 

 

On Sunday, July 9, 2023, 13-year-old Plaintiff Joseph Birkner (“Birkner”) and two companions climbed a perimeter fence and trespassed onto a closed middle school campus for the purpose of skateboarding.  During their excursion, Birkner scaled a caged vending machine and used the vending machine to climb onto the school roof.  Unfortunately, while on the roof, the 180-lb. Birkner walked across a skylight, which broke under Birkner’s weight.  Birkner fell through the skylight and suffered significant injuries.  

 

On April 2, 2024, Birkner, by and through Theresa Parham (“Parham”), his guardian ad litem, filed his original complaint against Defendant Los Angeles Unified School District (“LAUSD”). 

 

On May 28, 2024, Birkner filed his first amended complaint against LAUSD, alleging a single cause of action for negligence under Government Code section 835. 

 

On June 28, 2024, LAUSD filed its answer to the FAC. 

 

Also on June 28, 2024, Cross-Complainant LAUSD filed its cross-complaint against Cross-Defendants Birkner and Parham, seeking/alleging: (1) total equitable indemnity; (2) partial equitable indemnity; (3) declaratory relief; (4) equitable indemnity-liability of parents and guardians; and (5) relief under Education Code section 48904 (a)(1). 

 

On August 14, 2024, Cross-Defendants filed their answer to the cross-complaint. 

 

On¿November 13, 2025,¿the Court granted¿LAUSD’s¿motion for summary judgment¿as to Birkner’s¿FAC. 

 

On December 2, 2025, the Court entered judgment in favor of LAUSD and against Birkner. 

 

On February 4, 2026, Birkner filed his second amended complaint against Defendants LAUSD and John Valencia d/b/a Valen Vending Company (“Valencia”), alleging: (1) negligence under Government Code section 835; and (2) negligence. 

 

On February 20, 2026, Birkner filed his third amended complaint (the “TAC”) against Defendant Valencia, alleging a single cause of action for negligence. 

 

On May 12, 2026, LAUSD filed its motion for summary judgment or, alternatively, for summary adjudication of issues in the cross-complaint. 

 

On July 21, 2026, LAUSD filed its notice of Birkner’s non-opposition to the motion for summary judgment/summary adjudication. 

 

On July 22, 2026, Birkner filed his opposition brief. 

 

On July 24, 2026, LAUSD filed its reply brief. 

 

On July 31, 2026, the Court denied Birkner’s motion to reclassify this case as a limited civil action. 

 

As of 5:00 P.M. on August 3, 2026, nothing further had been filed in this matter by any party. 

 

B.  RULING 

 

None.  Instead, the Court will hear argument specifically on what evidence LAUSD submitted to establish that it met its burden.  In particular, the Court wants to hear from LAUSD about what prior Court findings were “necessarily” established in order to apply issue preclusion or collateral estoppel, as well as what evidence it submitted in addition to the prior ruling.

 

C.  LEGAL STANDARD 

 

The purpose of a motion for summary judgment “is to provide courts with a mechanism to cut through the parties’ pleadings in order to determine whether, despite their allegations, trial is in fact necessary to resolve their dispute.”¿ Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 843; Code Civ. Proc., § 437c (c).¿ Courts “liberally construe the evidence in support of the party opposing summary judgment or summary adjudication and resolve doubts concerning the evidence in favor of that party.”¿ Dore v. Arnold Worldwide, Inc. (2006) 39 Cal.4th 384, 389.¿ However, if all inferences reasonably deducible from the submitted evidence are uncontradicted by other inferences and there is no triable issue as to any material fact, the moving party is entitled to summary judgment as a matter of law.¿ Code Civ. Proc., § 437c (c); Adler v. Manor Healthcare Corp. (1992) 7 Cal.App.4th 1110, 1119. 

 

D  RULINGS ON OBJECTIONS TO EVIDENCE 

 

LAUSD objects to evidence submitted by Birkner in opposition to the motion.  Except as follows, the objections are not ruled upon, as, within the context of Avritt’s Declaration, they are not material to the Court’s decision.  To the extent anything in Avritt’s Declaration is material, the Court sustains each and every objection that is based on an improper legal conclusion, sustains each and every objection that is based on relevance and sustains each and every objection that is based on speculation and relevance.  The Court further adopts its prior rulings related to the same Declaration that was presented in relation to LAUSD’s earlier motion for summary judgment.

 

E.  DISCUSSION 

 

LAUSD moves for summary judgment or, alternatively, for summary adjudication of issues in the FAC. 

 

1.     The Court will not reject Birkner’s opposition brief or deny the motion on procedural grounds. 

 

LAUSD argues the Court should reject Birkner’s opposition brief because it was untimely filed.  While LAUSD is correct that Birkner’s opposition brief filed on July 22, 2026, was untimely (see Code Civ. Proc., § 437c (b)(2): opposition to summary judgment due 20 days before hearing), the Court elects to overlook this defect and evaluate the motion on its merits. 

The Court notes that Birkner failed to submit a separate statement of new material facts in support of his opposition brief.  Again, the Court elects to overlook this defect and evaluate the motion on its merits. 

 

2.     Allegations in the FAC 

 

Birkner’s complaint states that on July 9, 2023, he was attending school at John A. Sutter Middle School, which is owned and operated by LAUSD.  Birkner pleads that when he returned to the school after hours, he encountered dangerous and inviting conditions.  Birkner pleads the dangerous and inviting conditions constituted a substantial risk of injury to children on school property doing school related activities.  Birkner pleads the dangerous conditions were in an area owned, controlled, and maintained by LAUSD.  (FAC, ¶¶ 9-10.) 

 

Birkner pleads the school vending machine “was caged, which made it inviting to students, like Plaintiff, to climb and gain access to the School’s roof, thereby constituting a significant danger to young, curious school children near, around or otherwise encountering it.”  Birkner pleads “the School’s roof, in the area near (and above) the vending machine, was made up of faulty, unsecured plexiglass.”  Birkner pleads, “The caged vending machine encouraged Plaintiff to climb it and gain access to the School’s roof; once Plaintiff made it onto the roof, he proceeded to walk over the unsecured, ill-maintained plexiglass, which then shattered, caused Plaintiff to fall through and injure himself.”  (FAC, ¶ 9.)

 

3.   Allegations in the Cross-Complaint 

 

LAUSD pleads that on July 9, 2023, Birkner, a minor, went to John A. Sutter Middle School after hours, climbed a caged vending machine to get onto the roof, and fell through a plexiglass skylight.  LAUSD pleads Birkner injured himself and damaged school property.  LAUSD denies any responsibility.  (Cross-Complaint, ¶¶ 4-5, 16.) 

 

LAUSD pleads that Birkner’s own reckless conduct in breaking onto the roof caused his injuries.  LAUSD alleges Birkner’s family should have to cover LAUSD’s losses.  LAUSD alleges that because Parham was Birkner’s parent and had custody and control of Birkner at the time, Parham is legally responsible under Civil Code section 1714.1.  LAUSD wants Parham to share responsibility for damages that LAUSD pays because of Birkner’s actions.  (Cross-Complaint, ¶¶ 6-20.) 

 

LAUSD cites Education Code section 48904 (a)(1), which makes parents liable when their child willfully damages school property or injures someone at school up to a capped dollar amount.  LAUSD asks the Court to hold Birkner and Parham liable for the maximum amount allowed under that law.  (Cross-Complaint, ¶¶ 21-26.) 

 

4.     LAUSD’s Submitted Evidence 

 

LAUSD submits the following evidence in support of its motion: 

·        Copies of pleadings, orders, and a judgment entered in this case (Exhs. 1-4); 

·        A copy of LAUSD’s offer of dismissal in exchange for a waiver of costs and Birkner’s rejection thereof (Exh. 5); 

·        Excerpts from Birkner’s deposition transcript (Exh. 6); and 

·        The declaration of Julio Martinez and attached exhibit addressing the costs of repairing damage to the school. 

 

LAUSD’s submitted evidence shows:

·        Birkner sued LAUSD.  

·        Parham is Birkner’s mother and guardian ad litem.  

·        On November 13, 2025, the court granted LAUSD’s motion for summary judgment and entered a judgment in favor of LAUSD and against Birkner.  

(SUMF #1-4, 7.) 

 

LAUSD says that because of Birkner’s trespass, LAUSD needed to repair the broken skylight, which cost $3,813.33.  On March 4, 2026, LAUSD offered to dismiss its cross-complaint against Birkner in exchange for a waiver of LAUSD’s defense costs.  Birkner rejected the offer on March 6, 2026. (SUMF #5-6.) 

 

5.     LAUSD’s burden 

 

LAUSD moves for summary judgment of its claims in the cross-complaint: (1) total equitable indemnity; (2) partial equitable indemnity; (3) declaratory relief; (4) equitable indemnity-liability of parents and guardians; and (5) relief under Education Code section 48904 (a)(1). 

 

The thrust of LAUSD’s motion is that its submitted evidence bars relitigating the issue of Birkner’s negligence.  Specifically, LAUSD cites the Court’s order granting its motion for summary judgment as to the FAC as grounds for finding that the Court has already litigated issues surrounding Birkner’s negligence. 

 

LAUSD cites the following portions of the Court’s prior order granting LAUSD’s motion for summary judgment as to the FAC as supporting its position that issues regarding Birkner’s trespass and negligence have already been litigated: 

 

·        “Like the student in Bartell, Plaintiff was on school grounds ‘on his own volition and for his own amusement.’ Bartell, supra, 83 Cal.App.3d at p. 499.”  (Minute Order dated November 13, 2025, p. 11, ¶ 2.) 

·        “Plaintiff knew the school was a closed campus.”  (Minute Order dated November 13, 2025, p. 11, ¶ 1.) 

·        “The negligence in this case is attributable to the Plaintiff for making unreasonable decisions in knowingly trespassing, in accessing the roof using vending machine that had never been similarly used in 15 years, and in walking across a glass skylight. It is not the school district, but rather the Plaintiff who is at fault for this unfortunate incident. But for Plaintiff’s unreasonable (and unlawful) actions, Plaintiff would not have suffered injuries. No reasonable jury could find otherwise.”  (Minute Order dated November 13, 2025, p. 15, ¶ 3.) 

 

The doctrine of collateral estoppel bars relitigating issues actually litigated and necessarily decided in prior proceedings (Lucido v. Superior Court 51 Cal.3d 335, 341 (1990)). Five elements must be met: identical issue, actually litigated, necessarily decided, final decision on the merits, same party against whom preclusion is sought.

 

The problem with LAUSD’s motion is that, with the exception of negligence, it does not appear anything was necessarily decided previously by this Court.  And then it appears that LAUSD did not submit separate evidence supporting its cross-complaint.  So, for instance, no evidence, other than the prior order, was presented that Birker’s conduct was “willful.” Nor was evidence that an act was “intentional.”  Without such evidence, LAUSD did not meet its initial burden on all of its causes of action. (On Reply, LAUSD references various evidence it purportedly submitted on that issue; the Court would like LAUSD to point it to where that evidence was provided as part of the initial motion.)

 

If LAUSD is able to point the Court to evidence, the Court will then address Birker’s Opposition and LAUSD’s Reply. 

 

DATED: August 5, 2026 

 

_____________________ 

Lee S. Arian 

Judge of the Superior Court

[TENTATIVE] RULING RE: DEFENDANT’S MOTIONS TO COMPEL PLAINTIFF’S RESPONSES TO INITIAL DISCOVERY 

 

Dept. U 

8:30 a.m. 

August 5, 2026 

 

  1. BACKGROUND 

This case is a medical negligence action filed by Plaintiff Michael Benedetto against Defendant Bernard D. Monderer, M.D. 

On May 23, 2025, Plaintiff filed his complaint against Defendant, alleging: (1) medical negligence; (2) breach of fiduciary duty; (3) constructive fraud; and (4) lack of informed consent. 

On November 7, 2025, Judge Valerie Salkin overruled in part and sustained in part, with leave to amend, Defendant’s demurrer to the complaint.  The Court also granted, with leave to amend, Defendant’s motion to strike portions of the complaint.  Plaintiff did not file an amended complaint. 

On February 11, 2026, Defendant served Plaintiff with requests for production of documents (the “RFPs”), form interrogatories (the “FROGs”), and special interrogatories (the “SROGs”).  Despite Defendant’s subsequent efforts to meet and confer, Plaintiff failed to timely respond to the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs.  (Brandmeyer decl., ¶¶ 2-3.) 

On April 22, 2026, Defendant filed his motions to compel Plaintiff’s initial responses to the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs. 

As of 9:00 A.M. on July 3, 2026, Plaintiff had filed no opposition brief. 

  1. RULING 

The motions are granted.  No sanctions will issue at this time. 

  1. LEGAL STANDARD  

  1. Motion to Compel Initial Responses to Requests for Production of Documents 

Where there has been no response to a demand to produce documents, the demanding party may seek an order compelling a response.¿ Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.300. 

  1. Motion to Compel Initial Responses to Interrogatories  

If a party to whom interrogatories are directed fails to serve a timely response, the demanding party may move for an order compelling a response.¿ Code Civ. Proc., § 2030.290. 

  1. DISCUSSION 

Defendant moves to compel Plaintiff’s initial responses to the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs. 

On February 11, 2026, Defendant served the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs on Plaintiff.  Despite Defendant’s efforts to meet and confer, Plaintiff failed to timely respond to the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs.  Defendant is entitled to an order compelling Plaintiff to respond to the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs, without stating objections, within thirty (30) days.  See Code Civ. Proc., §§ 2030.290, 2031.300. 

Defendant does not request attorneys’ fees.  No sanctions will issue at this time. 

  1. CONCLUSION  

Plaintiff Michael Benedetto is ORDERED to provide initial responses to Defendant Bernard D. Monderer, M.D.’s Requests for Production of Documents, Form Interrogatories, and Special Interrogatories, without stating objections, within thirty (30) days of this order. 

 

No sanctions will issue at this time. 

 

Defendant Bernard D. Monderer, M.D. is ORDERED to give notice. 

 

DATED: August 5, 2026

Judge of the Superior Court

[TENTATIVE] RULING RE: OSC RE: PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION 

 

Dept. U 

8:30 a.m. 

August 5, 2026 

 

  1. BACKGROUND 

This case is a quiet title action arising from an alleged wrongful foreclosure sale. 

On January 8, 2026, Plaintiff 9000 Arlington Ave LLC filed its complaint against Defendants Richard Irwin Kane (“Kane”), Trustee of The Richard Irwin Kane 2006 Trust; Bronzetree Terraces, LLC (“Bronzetree”); RTI Properties, Inc. (“RTI”); Rediger Investment Mortgage Fund (“Rediger”); Peak Foreclosure Services, Inc. (“Peak”); and Lida Kohansameh (“Kohansameh”), alleging: (1) wrongful foreclosure; (2) cancellation of instruments; (3) promissory estoppel; and (4) quiet title. 

On January 13, 2026, Plaintiff filed a notice of recording lis pendens against real property that is the subject of this action. 

On January 21, 2026, Kohansameh filed her answer to the complaint. 

On March 3, 2026, Plaintiff dismissed Rediger as a defendant from this case. 

On June 1, 2026, Kohansameh filed her application for a temporary restraining order (“TRO”) and order to show cause (“OSC”) re: preliminary injunction. 

Also on June 1, 2026, Plaintiff filed its opposition brief. 

On June 2, 2026, Judge Anthony Mohr granted in part Kohansameh’s application for a TRO and entered an order that Plaintiff be, among other things, “immediately restrained and enjoined from performing, directing, permitting, or causing any construction, alteration, or work of any kind at 23476 Palm Drive, Calabasas, California 91302, pending further order.”  (Order dated June 2, 2026, ¶ 1.)  Judge Mohr declined to issue part of Kohansameh’s proposed order that would require Plaintiff to immediately vacate the property. 

On June 12, 2026, Judge Mohr set a hearing on an OSC re: preliminary injunction for July 6, 2026. 

On June 17, 2026, Kohansameh filed an attorney declaration in support of her request for an order continuing the hearing on the OSC re: preliminary injunction. 

On June 23, 2026, Judge Yolanda Orozco sustained, with leave to amend, Kane’s demurrer to the complaint and granted, with leave to amend, Kane’s motion to strike portions of the complaint. 

On July 6, 2026, the Court entered the parties’ joint stipulation to continue the hearing on the OSC re: preliminary injunction to August 5, 2026. 

On July 14, 2026, Plaintiff filed its first amended complaint against Kane, Bronzetree, RTI, Peak, and Kohansameh, alleging: (1) wrongful foreclosure; (2) cancellation of instruments; (3) promissory estoppel; and (4) quiet title. 

On July 17, 2026, Kohansameh posted a $10,000.00 bond as required under Judge Mohr’s TRO. 

On July 27, 2026, Kohansameh filed another supplemental attorney declaration in support of her request for a preliminary injunction. 

On July 31, 2026, Plaintiff filed objections to evidence. 

As of 10:00 A.M. on August 4, 2026, nothing further had been filed in this matter by any party. 

  1. RULING 

The application for preliminary injunction is denied.  The TRO is dissolved. 

  1. LEGAL STANDARD 

The purpose of a preliminary injunction is to preserve the¿status quo¿and prevent¿irreparable harm pending a trial on the merits.¿¿White v. Davis¿(2003) 30 Cal.4th 528, 554.¿¿To obtain a¿preliminary injunction, a¿moving party¿must show: (1) she would likely suffer an irreparable injury for which damages would be an inadequate remedy if the injunction¿were¿denied; and (2) there exists a¿reasonable¿probability that she will prevail on the merits of her claims.¿¿Huong¿Que, Inc. v. Luu¿(2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 400, 408. 

  1. RULINGS ON OBJECTIONS TO EVIDENCE 

Plaintiff objects to evidence submitted by Kohansameh in support of her request for a preliminary injunction.  Plaintiff’s objections are overruled, except that the Court has considered Mr. Hofman’s lack of an expert witness designation and lack of personal knowledge of facts stated in his most recent supplemental attorney declaration.  The Court’s analysis of Mr. Hofman’s most recent supplemental attorney declaration is included herein. 

  1. DISCUSSION 

After Judge Mohr issued a TRO, Kohansameh filed no supplemental brief to clarify her position as to why a preliminary injunction should issue.  Rather, Kohansameh’s supplemental attorney declarations appear to indicate that the preliminary injunction issue is moot. 

On June 17, 2026, counsel for Kohansameh filed a declaration stating that the outcome of a separately pending unlawful detainer action involving the same property and the same parties “could alter the necessity of a preliminary injunction” if she obtained a favorable result on a motion for summary judgment set for hearing on July 8, 2026.  (Hofman decl. dated June 17, 2026, ¶ 3.) 

On July 27, 2026, counsel for Kohansameh filed a second declaration stating that he had personally inspected the premises and that, to his eye, “[i]t looked as if someone had abandoned the premises.”  (Hofman decl. dated July 27, 2026, ¶ 3.)  Counsel continues, “The moving party herein has already prevailed on summary judgment in the unlawful detainer action and is just awaiting the final conclusion of the lock out.”  (Hofman decl. dated July 27, 2026, ¶ 6.)  Counsel requests, without legal reasoning, that Plaintiff be required to post a $10 million bond unless it has “formally moved out by August 4, 2026.”  (Hofman decl. dated July 27, 2026, ¶ 8.) 

Counsel for Kohansameh goes on to state that in his non-expert opinion, the lack of maintenance at the premises presents health and safety concerns and a fire risk.  Counsel does not state the specific bases for his non-expert opinion that the condition of the premises presents a fire risk.  In short, counsel is unqualified to provide credible opinion as to such risks, and the Court disregards his testimony in these regards.  Even if counsel were qualified to provide such an expert opinion, Kohansameh fails to explain how a continuing injunction is necessary to abate such risks if Plaintiff has already moved out and Kohansameh already has access to the premises. 

In sum, Kohansameh concedes that she has already prevailed in the separately pending unlawful detainer action and that Plaintiff has already vacated the premises.  Thus, there is no risk that Plaintiff’s continued possession of the premises will result in irreparable harm.  (Again, the Court disregards counsel’s non-expert testimony that there is an immediate fire risk.)  By all appearances, the application for preliminary injunction is moot, as is any need to continue the TRO.   

The application for preliminary injunction is denied.  The TRO is dissolved. 

  1. CONCLUSION 

Defendant Lida Kohansameh’s application for a preliminary injunction is DENIED. 

 

The Temporary Restraining Order issued by Judge Anthony Mohr on June 2, 2026, is DISSOLVED. 

 

The Clerk is ORDERED to give notice. 

 

DATED: August 5, 2026
